claim: CEP78 is a causative gene of cone-rod dystrophy (CRD) and male infertility with multiple morphological abnormalities of sperm flagella (MMAF) in both human and mouse.
source: Here, we report CEP78 as a causative gene of a particular syndrome including CRD and male infertility with multiple morphological abnormalities of sperm flagella (MMAF) both in human and mouse.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Cep78 knockout mice and a human patient with CEP78 mutation, showing both CRD and MMAF phenotypes.

claim: Cep78 knockout mice exhibited reduced ERG amplitudes.
source: Scotopic a- and b-wave and photopic b-wave amplitudes were reduced in Cep78−/− mice when compared to age-matched Cep78+/− mice (Figure 1A–E).
evidence: ERG measurements from Cep78−/− mice at multiple ages showed reduced amplitudes compared to controls, as shown in Figure 1A-E.

claim: Scotopic a-wave amplitudes showed approximately 13.6, 39.1, 40.8, and 64.8% decrease in Cep78−/− mice at 3, 6, 9, and 18 months, respectively.
source: According to our data, amplitudes of scotopic a-wave showed approximately 13.6, 39.1, 40.8, and 64.8% decrease in Cep78−/− mice at 3, 6, 9, and 18 months, respectively (Figure 1A and C)
evidence: Quantitative ERG data from Figure 1A and C showing specific percentage decreases at different ages.

claim: Scotopic b-wave amplitudes were downregulated by 19.9, 30.5, 35.6, and 58.3% in Cep78−/− mice at 3, 6, 9, and 18 months, respectively.
source: amplitudes of scotopic b-wave were downregulated by 19.9, 30.5, 35.6, and 58.3% in Cep78−/− mice at 3, 6, 9, and 18 months, respectively (Figure 1A and D).
evidence: Quantitative ERG data from Figure 1A and D showing specific percentage decreases at different ages.

claim: Photopic b-wave amplitudes were decreased by 39.4, 39.8, 52.8, and 69.0% in Cep78−/− mice at 3, 6, 9, and 18 months, respectively.
source: Similarly, amplitudes of photopic b-wave were decreased by 39.4, 39.8, 52.8, and 69.0% in Cep78−/− mice at 3, 6, 9, and 18 months, respectively (Figure 1B and E).
evidence: Quantitative ERG data from Figure 1B and E showing specific percentage decreases at different ages.

claim: Light-induced translocation of cone arrestin in Cep78−/− mice retina was slower and more limited than in Cep78+/− mice.
source: Light exposure of 2 hr triggered a shift of cone arrestin from the inner cellular compartments to the OS in both Cep78+/− and Cep78−/− mice. However, light-induced translocation of cone arrestin in Cep78−/− mice retina was slower and more limited than in Cep78+/− mice (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: Immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 1F-G demonstrating reduced cone arrestin translocation in Cep78−/− mice.

claim: Thicknesses of outer nuclear layer (ONL) were attenuated in Cep78−/− mice when compared to Cep78+/− mice at ages of 3, 9, and 12 months.
source: SD-OCT showed that thicknesses of ONL were attenuated in Cep78−/− mice when compared to Cep78+/− mice at ages of 3, 9, and 12 months (Figure 1H–K).
evidence: SD-OCT imaging data from Figure 1H-K showing reduced ONL thickness at multiple time points.

claim: Disorganized, sparse, and caduceus photoreceptor OS disks and widened OS bases were observed in Cep78−/− mice.
source: However, disorganized, sparse, and caduceus photoreceptor OS disks and widened OS bases were observed in age-matched Cep78−/− mice (Figure 1L).
evidence: TEM images in Figure 1L showing ultrastructural abnormalities in photoreceptor outer segments.

claim: Connecting cilia are shortened in Cep78−/− mice at 3-, 6-, and 9-month age compared to age-matched Cep78+/−.
source: Our data indicate that connecting cilia are shortened in Cep78−/− mice at 3-, 6-, and 9-month age compared to age-matched Cep78+/− (Figure 2B).
evidence: Immunofluorescence and TEM data from Figure 2B showing quantified reduction in connecting cilium length.

claim: Swelled upper part and disorganized microtubules in connecting cilia of Cep78−/− mice were observed.
source: Moreover, we observed swelled upper part and disorganized microtubules in connecting cilia of Cep78−/− mice (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: TEM images in Figure 2E-G showing structural abnormalities in connecting cilia.

claim: Structures of basal bodies, adjacent daughter centrioles, or other organelles of inner segment were not altered in Cep78−/− mice.
source: However, structures of basal bodies, adjacent daughter centrioles, or other organelles of inner segment were not altered in Cep78−/− mice (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: TEM images in Figure 2E-G showing normal structures of basal bodies and other organelles.

claim: Cep78−/− male mice were infertile.
source: Mating test with Cep78+/− female mice for 3 months showed that Cep78−/− male mice were infertile (Figure 3A).
evidence: Mating test data shown in Figure 3A demonstrating zero fertility in Cep78−/− males.

claim: Sperm concentration, motility, and progressive motility were decreased upon Cep78 deletion.
source: To further explore the underlying causes of male infertility of Cep78−/− mice, we assessed the concentration, motility, and progressive motility of sperm isolated from cauda epididymis using computer-assisted sperm analysis (CASA), and all three parameters were decreased upon Cep78 deletion (Table 1, Figure 1—video 1 and Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: CASA data presented in Table 1 showing reduced sperm parameters in Cep78−/− mice.

claim: Spermatozoa with abnormal heads, necks, and flagella accounted for 92.10, 82.61 and 95.67% of total spermatozoa, respectively, in Cep78−/− male mice.
source: Spermatozoa with abnormal heads, necks, and flagella accounted for 92.10, 82.61 and 95.67% of total spermatozoa, respectively, in Cep78−/− male mice (Table 1).
evidence: Morphological analysis data presented in Table 1 showing high percentages of abnormal sperm.

claim: A total of 806 downregulated proteins and 80 upregulated proteins were identified upon Cep78 depletion in elongating spermatids.
source: We set the threshold as a fold-change greater than 1.5 and p value less than 0.05 and identified a total of 806 downregulated proteins and 80 upregulated proteins upon Cep78 depletion, which were visualized using hierarchical clustering analyses (Figure 3N and Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Mass spectrometry data from elongating spermatids showing differential protein expression, visualized in Figure 3N.

claim: Significantly enriched gene ontology terms in cellular components included sperm principal piece, sperm fibrous sheath, acrosomal vesicle, motile cilium, centrosome, microtubule skeleton, and dynein complex.
source: Consistent with above findings in morphological anomalies in sperm, significantly enriched gene ontology terms in cellular components included sperm principal piece, sperm fibrous sheath, acrosomal vesicle, motile cilium, centrosome, microtubule skeleton, and dynein complex (Figure 3O and Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Gene ontology analysis of mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3O.

claim: Flagellar formation defects were observed from stages I–III to stages VII–VIII during spermatogenesis in Cep78−/− testes.
source: Light microscopy showed an apparent scarcity of sperm flagella visible in the lumens of Cep78−/− testes (Figure 4A–B), with flagellar formation defects observed from stages I–III to stages VII–VIII during spermatogenesis (Figure 4B)
evidence: PAS staining data shown in Figure 4A-B demonstrating flagellar defects at specific spermatogenesis stages.

claim: Disordered mitochondria and a jumble of unassembled flagellar components were present in Cep78−/− sperm.
source: However, disordered mitochondria and a jumble of unassembled flagellar components were present in Cep78−/− sperm (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: TEM images in Figure 4E-F showing ultrastructural abnormalities in sperm.

claim: Cep78−/− sperm showed complete derangement of ODF and scattered '9+2' microtubules.
source: In contrast, Cep78−/− sperm showed complete derangement of ODF and scattered '9+2' microtubules (Figure 4I–J).
evidence: TEM cross-section images in Figure 4I-J showing disrupted microtubule organization.

claim: Triplet microtubules were found at both middle and principal pieces of sperm flagella in Cep78−/− sperm.
source: In Cep78−/− sperm, triplet microtubules, which were supposed to exist only in proximal centrioles, were found at both middle and principal pieces of sperm flagella (Figure 4I–J)
evidence: TEM images in Figure 4I-J showing triplet microtubules in abnormal locations.

claim: Depletion of Cep78 promoted centriole elongation in spermatids.
source: Two-dot staining pattern of disengaged centrioles was observed in Cep78+/− spermatids (Figure 4K), while depletion of Cep78 promoted centriole elongation in spermatids (Figure 4K)
evidence: Immunofluorescence staining data in Figure 4K showing elongated centrioles in Cep78−/− spermatids.

claim: Cep78−/− testes exhibit abnormal club-shaped nuclear morphology of elongated spermatids since step 10.
source: In addition to axonemal defects in sperm flagella, Cep78−/− testes also exhibit deformation of spermatid nuclei, as evidenced by abnormal club-shaped nuclear morphology of elongated spermatids since step 10, in contrast to the normal hook-shaped head in Cep78+/− elongated spermatids (Figure 4B, Figure 5A).
evidence: PAS staining data in Figure 4B and Figure 5A showing abnormal nuclear morphology.

claim: Abnormal elongation of manchette structures in testicular spermatids of Cep78−/− mice during spermiogenesis was observed.
source: Abnormal elongation of manchette structures in testicular spermatids of Cep78−/− mice during spermiogenesis was also shown by immunofluorescence staining (Figure 5B)
evidence: Immunofluorescence staining data in Figure 5B showing abnormal manchette structures.

claim: Nuclear condensing was normal in Cep78−/− spermatids.
source: TEM suggested that nuclear condensing was normal in Cep78−/− spermatids (Figure 5D–F– and K–M).
evidence: TEM images in Figure 5D-F and K-M showing normal nuclear condensation.

claim: Cep78 loss does not affect spermatocyte development at leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, and diplotene stages.
source: Our results show Cep78 loss does not affect spermatocyte development at all four stages (Figure 5O–P), implying that Cep78 deletion exerted no effect on the prophase of meiosis I.
evidence: Spermatocyte spreading data in Figure 5O-P showing no difference in meiotic stages.

claim: Various abnormalities in manchette formation and acrosomal biogenesis were revealed in Cep78−/− spermatids.
source: We herein revealed various abnormalities in manchette formation and acrosomal biogenesis in Cep78−/− spermatids, including an abnormal nuclear constriction at the site of perinuclear rings (Figure 5D), ectopic and asymmetric perinuclear rings together with disordered manchette microtubules (Figure 5E–F– and K), abnormal acrosome and nuclei invagination (Figure 5L), and detached acrosome from nuclear membrane (Figure 5M).
evidence: TEM images in Figure 5D-M showing multiple ultrastructural abnormalities.

claim: CEP78 c.1629–2A>G mutation leads to loss of CEP78 protein.
source: Our immunoblotting results reveal neither full length CEP78 protein nor truncated CEP78 protein in white blood cells of patient carrying CEP78 c.1629–2A>G mutation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that this mutation leads to loss of CEP78 protein.
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 showing absence of CEP78 protein in patient.

claim: The male patient carrying CEP78 c.1629–2A>G mutation was infertile.
source: The patient was infertile.
evidence: Clinical observation of the patient with CEP78 mutation.

claim: CASA revealed obvious reductions in sperm concentration, motility, and progressive motility in the CEP78-mutated man.
source: However, CASA revealed obvious reductions in sperm concentration, motility, and progressive motility in the CEP78-mutated man according to the standard of the WHO guidelines (Table 1).
evidence: CASA data presented in Table 1 showing reduced sperm parameters in the patient.

claim: The patient's sperm showed typical MMAF phenotypes, such as abnormal heads (95.42%), necks (85.62%), and flagella (97.39%).
source: The patient's semen sample was further submitted for morphological analyses using light microscopy and SEM, both of which showed typical MMAF phenotypes, such as abnormal heads (95.42%), necks (85.62%), and flagella (97.39%; Figure 6A–J and Table 1).
evidence: Morphological analysis data presented in Table 1 and Figure 6A-J showing high percentages of abnormal sperm.

claim: Multiple ultra-structural abnormalities were observed in the spermatozoa of the patient carrying CEP78 c.1629–2A>G mutation.
source: Based on our data, multiple ultra-structural abnormalities were observed in the spermatozoa of case as compared to those of age-matched healthy male individual (Figure 6K–R).
evidence: TEM images in Figure 6K-R showing ultrastructural abnormalities in patient sperm.

claim: Triplet microtubules unique to proximal centrioles in sperms were observed in both principal and middle pieces of patient's sperm flagella.
source: Similar to the Cep78−/− mice data, triplet microtubules unique to proximal centrioles in sperms were also observed in both principal and middle pieces of patient's sperm flagella (Figure 6P and R).
evidence: TEM images in Figure 6P and R showing triplet microtubules in abnormal locations in patient sperm.

claim: A total of 16 ciliary proteins were initially screened out by proteomic analyses of Cep78 immunoprecipitation.
source: A total of 16 ciliary proteins were initially screened out by proteomic analyses (Table 2)
evidence: IP-MS data presented in Table 2 identifying Cep78 interacting proteins.

claim: CEP78 interacted with IFT20.
source: Protein interactions between CEP78 and IFT20 (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: Co-IP data in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A demonstrating protein-protein interaction.

claim: CEP78 interacted with TTC21A.
source: CEP78 and TTC21A (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: Co-IP data in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2B demonstrating protein-protein interaction.

claim: IFT20 and TTC21A interact with each other.
source: and IFT20 and TTC21A (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 2C) were identified
evidence: Co-IP data in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2C demonstrating protein-protein interaction.

claim: The binding between Ift20 and Ttc21a was severely disrupted upon Cep78 knockout.
source: As revealed by co-IP and immunoblotting results, the binding between Ift20 and Ttc21a was severely disrupted upon Cep78 knockout (Figure 7D)
evidence: Co-IP data in Figure 7D showing reduced interaction between Ift20 and Ttc21a in Cep78−/− mice.

claim: Endogenous testicular Cep78, Ift20, and Ttc21a proteins were co-fractionated in a complex ranging in size of 158–670 kDa.
source: Meanwhile, the size exclusion chromatography result demonstrated that endogenous testicular Cep78, Ift20, and Ttc21a proteins were co-fractionated in a complex ranging in size of 158–670 kDa (Figure 7E).
evidence: Size exclusion chromatography data in Figure 7E showing co-fractionation of the three proteins.

claim: Ift20 and Ttc21a localized peripheral to Cep78 at the top view of the centriole.
source: our 3D structured illumination microscopy (SIM) showed that Ift20 and Ttc21a localized peripheral to Cep78 at the top view of the centriole, and Ift20 and Ttc21a co-localized at one end of Cep78-positive centriole part (Figure 7F).
evidence: 3D-SIM imaging data in Figure 7F showing spatial localization of the three proteins.

claim: Expression of both Ttc21a and Ift20 decreased in testes of Cep78−/− mice compared to Cep78+/− mice.
source: In addition, we found that expression of both Ttc21a and Ift20 decreased in testes of Cep78−/− mice compared to Cep78+/− mice (Figure 7G–I).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 7G-I showing reduced protein levels of Ttc21a and Ift20 in Cep78−/− testes.

claim: Decreased Ttc21a and Ift20 protein levels were observed in Cep78 siRNA transfected NIH3T3 cells.
source: Similarly, decreased Ttc21a and Ift20 protein levels were observed in Cep78 siRNA transfected NIH3T3 cells compared with cells transfected with scramble siRNA (Figure 7J–M and Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 7J-M showing reduced protein levels after Cep78 knockdown.

claim: Cilium length was reduced after Cep78, Ift20, or Ttc21a knockdown.
source: we found that cilium length was reduced after Cep78, Ift20, or Ttc21a knockdown (Figure 7N and O)
evidence: Immunofluorescence data in Figure 7N and O showing shortened cilia after knockdown of each protein.

claim: Centrioles were longer in NIH3T3 cells with Cep78 or Ift20 knockdown.
source: We found that the centrioles were longer in NIH3T3 cells with Cep78 or Ift20 knockdown, and the length changes were reverted by overexpression of Cep78syn-HA and Ift20syn-Flag (Figure 7P and Q).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data in Figure 7P and Q showing elongated centrioles after Cep78 or Ift20 knockdown.

claim: No change in centriole length was observed after Ttc21a knockdown or rescue.
source: However, we observed no change in centriole length after Ttc21a knockdown or rescue (Figure 7P and Q).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data in Figure 7P and Q showing no effect of Ttc21a on centriole length.

claim: The centriolar localization of Ift20 protein was disrupted after Cep78 knockdown.
source: Additionally, we also observed that the centriolar localization of Ift20 protein was disrupted after Cep78 knockdown (Figure 7R and S)
evidence: Immunofluorescence data in Figure 7R and S showing altered Ift20 localization after Cep78 knockdown.

claim: Depletion of Cep78 downregulated Ift20 and Ttc21a.
source: and depletion of Cep78 downregulated Ift20 and Ttc21a (Figure 7G, H, J and M)
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 7G, H, J and M showing reduced protein levels.

claim: Knockdown of Ift20 or Ttc21a did not significantly affect the protein level of Cep78 and other interacting proteins.
source: while knockdown of Ift20 or Ttc21a did not significantly affect the protein level of Cep78 and other interacting proteins (Figure 7—figure supplement 3D, F, G, H, J, K)
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 7—figure supplement 3D, F, G, H, J, K showing no effect on Cep78 levels.

claim: CEP78 is a centriolar protein composed of 722 amino acids and possesses two leucine-rich repeat regions and a coiled-coil domain.
source: Centrosomal protein of 78 kDa (CEP78), protein encoded by the CEP78 gene (MIM: 617110), is a centriolar protein composed of 722 amino acids and possesses two leucine-rich repeat regions and a coiled-coil domain (Brunk et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brunk et al., 2016.

claim: CEP78 localizes to the distal region of mature centrioles.
source: CEP78 localizes to the distal region of mature centrioles and is exclusively expressed in ciliated organisms, supporting its crucial function in maintaining centrosome homeostasis (Hossain, 2017; Azimzadeh et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hossain, 2017 and Azimzadeh et al., 2012.

claim: Mutations in the CEP78 gene cause autosomal recessive CRDHL.
source: Mutations in the CEP78 gene cause autosomal recessive CRDHL (MIM: 617236; Fu, 2017; Nikopoulos et al., 2016; Namburi et al., 2016; Sanchis-Juan et al., 2018; Ascari et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including Fu, 2017; Nikopoulos et al., 2016; Namburi et al., 2016; Sanchis-Juan et al., 2018; Ascari et al., 2020.

claim: Deregulation of Cep78 contributes to colorectal cancer, prostate cancer, and asthenoteratozoospermia.
source: Deregulation of Cep78 also contributes to colorectal cancer (Zhang et al., 2016a), prostate cancer (Nesslinger et al., 2007), and asthenoteratozoospermia (Ascari et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2016a; Nesslinger et al., 2007; and Ascari et al., 2020.

claim: CEP78 functions downstream of CEP350 to control biogenesis of primary cilia.
source: As a centrosomal protein, CEP78 functions downstream of CEP350 to control biogenesis of primary cilia (Gonçalves et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gonçalves et al., 2021.

claim: CEP78 regulates centrosome homeostasis through interactions with other centrosomal proteins, including CEP76, CP110, and EDD-DYRK2-DDB1VprBP.
source: and regulates centrosome homeostasis through interactions with other centrosomal proteins, including CEP76, CP110, and EDD-DYRK2-DDB1VprBP (Hossain, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hossain, 2017.

claim: IFT20 and TTC21A are both IFT proteins interacting with each other and vital for spermatogenesis and cilliogenesis.
source: IFT20 and TTC21A are both IFT proteins interacting with each other and vital for spermatogenesis and cilliogenesis (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2019.

claim: IFT20 is part of IFT-B subcomplex.
source: IFT20 is part of IFT-B subcomplex (Petriman et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Petriman et al., 2022.

claim: TTC21A is part of IFT-A complex.
source: while TTC21A is part of IFT-A complex (Hesketh et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hesketh et al., 2022.

claim: IFT20 and TTC21A are vital for spermatogenesis and cilliogenesis.
source: We found that CEP78 interacted with IFT20 and TTC21A, which are vital for spermatogenesis and cilliogenesis (Liu et al., 2019; Keady et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2016a)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2019; Keady et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2016a.

claim: In normal retina, light exposure drives rapid movement of cone arrestin into outer segments (OS) of cone photoreceptors.
source: In normal retina, light exposure drives rapid movement of cone arrestin into outer segments (OS) of cone photoreceptors (Zhu et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2002.

claim: CEP250 mutation is related to CRD and hearing loss (CRDHL).
source: CEP250 mutation is related to CRD and hearing loss (CRDHL; Kubota et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kubota et al., 2018.

claim: CEP19 mutation is related to CRD with obesity and renal malformation.
source: and CEP19 mutation to CRD with obesity and renal malformation (Yıldız Bölükbaşı et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yıldız Bölükbaşı et al., 2018.

claim: The manchette structure regulates sperm head formation during spermiogenesis.
source: The manchette structure, consisting of a series of parallel microtubule bundles that extend from perinuclear rings of nucleus to distal cytoplasm and are closely proximity to or parallel to nuclear membranes, regulates sperm head formation during spermiogenesis (Kierszenbaum and Tres, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kierszenbaum and Tres, 2004.

claim: Manchette microtubules are nucleated at spermatid centrosomes.
source: Most views hold that manchette microtubules are nucleated at spermatid centrosomes (Lehti and Sironen, 2016; Kierszenbaum et al., 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lehti and Sironen, 2016 and Kierszenbaum et al., 2002.

claim: Manchette microtubules start from nucleator γ-tubulin of the centrosomal adjunct and end at perinuclear rings.
source: which start from nucleator γ-tubulin of the centrosomal adjunct and end at perinuclear rings (Akhmanova et al., 2005; Kierszenbaum et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Akhmanova et al., 2005 and Kierszenbaum et al., 2011.

claim: IFT20 is required for opsin trafficking and photoreceptor OS development.
source: It is required for opsin trafficking and photoreceptor OS development (Keady et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Keady et al., 2011.

claim: During spermiogenesis, IFT20 is transported along the manchette microtubules.
source: During spermiogenesis, IFT20 is transported along the manchette microtubules (Kazarian et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kazarian et al., 2018.

claim: Multiple sperm flagella abnormalities are observed in Ift20 mutant mice, including short and kinked tails.
source: Multiple sperm flagella abnormalities are observed in Ift20 mutant mice, including short and kinked tails (Zhang et al., 2016a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2016a.

claim: Mutations in TTC21A gene are reported to cause MMAF in both human and mice.
source: TTC21A interacts with IFT20, and mutations in TTC21A gene are reported to cause MMAF in both human and mice (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2019.

claim: CEP78 protein is highly conserved in vertebrate organisms with human and mouse CEP78 proteins sharing over 80% similarity.
source: CEP78 protein is highly conserved in vertebrate organisms with human and mouse CEP78 proteins sharing over 80% similarity.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about protein conservation.

claim: Cep78 is involved at the stage of sperm flagellar formation.
source: Light microscopy showed an apparent scarcity of sperm flagella visible in the lumens of Cep78−/− testes (Figure 4A–B), with flagellar formation defects observed from stages I–III to stages VII–VIII during spermatogenesis (Figure 4B), suggesting that Cep78 was involved at the stage of sperm flagellar formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of flagellar defects at specific spermatogenesis stages.

claim: Triplet microtubules in principal and middle pieces of sperm flagella are indicative of abnormal elongation of centrioles during sperm flagella formation.
source: In Cep78−/− sperm, triplet microtubules, which were supposed to exist only in proximal centrioles, were found at both middle and principal pieces of sperm flagella (Figure 4I–J), indicative of abnormal elongation of centrioles during sperm flagella formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of triplet microtubules in abnormal locations.

claim: Centriole anomalies are potential causative factors of deregulation of sperm development in mouse.
source: The various types of aberrant sperm flagella observed in mice with Cep78 defects, together with the triplet microtubules found in principal and middle pieces of sperm flagella upon Cep78 deletion, suggested centriole anomalies as potential causative factors of deregulation of sperm development in mouse.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple observations of centriole and flagellar abnormalities.

claim: Cep78 regulates centriole structures and functions.
source: Two-dot staining pattern of disengaged centrioles was observed in Cep78+/− spermatids (Figure 4K), while depletion of Cep78 promoted centriole elongation in spermatids (Figure 4K), supporting the role of Cep78 in regulating centriole structures and functions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of centriole elongation upon Cep78 depletion.

claim: The defective spermatid manchette formation in Cep78−/− mice led to peculiar shaping of nucleus and abnormal sperm head formation.
source: The defective spermatid manchette formation in Cep78−/− mice led to peculiar shaping of nucleus and abnormal sperm head formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of manchette defects and abnormal head morphology.

claim: Cep78 may regulate formation of sperm flagellum by a different mechanism than CP110.
source: We found that CEP78 loss led to shortening of sperm flagellum, with Cp110 downregulated in Cep78−/− testis (Figure 7—figure supplement 5), which is inconsistent with Gonçalves et al., 2021's findings that cells lacking CEP78 display upregulated CP110 and reduced cilia frequency with long cilia phenotype (Gonçalves et al., 2021). It seems that Cep78 may regulate formation of sperm flagellum by a different mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the discrepancy between findings in sperm and previous cell culture studies.

claim: Insufficiency of Cep78 and any interacting proteins disrupts its structure and affects stability of all components, leading to cilia shortening.
source: Insufficiency of Cep78 and any interacting proteins disrupts its structure and affects stability of all components, leading to cilia shortening.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that loss of Cep78 reduces levels of interacting proteins and shortens cilia.

claim: Cep78 maintains centriole homeostasis and cilliogenesis by recruiting Ift20 and Ttc21a.
source: indicating that Cep78 maintains centriole homeostasis and cilliogenesis by recruiting Ift20 and Ttc21a.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Cep78 affects localization and levels of Ift20 and Ttc21a, but not vice versa.

claim: Cep78−/− mice model is an applicable animal model for therapeutic research of CRD and male infertility syndrome.
source: Our study also reveals Cep78−/− mice model as an applicable animal model for therapeutic research of such a distinct syndrome.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of phenotypes between human and mouse.

claim: Expression of Cep78 protein was completely absent in the neural retina and testes of Cep78−/− mice.
source: As revealed by immunoblotting, expression of Cep78 protein was completely absent in the neural retina and testes of Cep78−/− mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D), indicating successful generation of Cep78 knockout mice.
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D showing absence of Cep78 protein.

claim: The reduction in ERG amplitudes extended as age increased in Cep78−/− mice.
source: The reduction extended as age increased.
evidence: This is observed from the progressive decrease in ERG amplitudes at 3, 6, 9, and 18 months.

claim: The attenuation of ONL thickness became more evident along with increase of age in Cep78−/− mice.
source: The attenuation became more evident along with increase of age (Figure 1H–K).
evidence: SD-OCT data in Figure 1H-K showing progressive thinning of ONL with age.

claim: Both functions and morphologies of mice photoreceptor are disturbed upon Cep78 deletion.
source: Collectively, our results indicate that both functions and morphologies of mice photoreceptor are disturbed upon Cep78 deletion.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on ERG, immunofluorescence, SD-OCT, and TEM data.

claim: Cep78 deficiency interrupts cilia elongation and disturbed ciliary structures in photoreceptors.
source: Together, our data show that Cep78 deficiency interrupts cilia elongation and disturbed ciliary structures in photoreceptors.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on immunofluorescence and TEM data of connecting cilia.

claim: Cep78 deletion decreases count, motility and progressive motility of sperm, morphological abnormalities of sperm head, and flagella in mice, as well as dysregulated sperm proteins, thus accounting for male infertility.
source: Taken together, Cep78 deletion decreases count, motility and progressive motility of sperm, morphological abnormalities of sperm head, and flagella in mice, as well as dysregulated sperm proteins, thus accounting for male infertility.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on CASA, morphological analysis, and mass spectrometry data.

claim: Defective microtubule arrangements and elongated centrioles are present in sperm flagella of Cep78−/− mice.
source: Collectively, our data reveal defective microtubule arrangements and elongated centrioles in sperm flagella of Cep78+/− mice.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on TEM and immunofluorescence data of sperm.

claim: The absence of Cep78 generates defective spermatid head formation.
source: Therefore, the above findings indicate that the absence of Cep78 generates defective spermatid head formation.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on PAS staining, immunofluorescence, and TEM data of spermatid head formation.

claim: The patient carrying CEP78 c.1629–2A>G mutation presented typical MMAF phenotypes.
source: Taken together, this patient carrying CEP78 c.1629–2A>G mutation presented typical MMAF phenotypes.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on CASA, morphological analysis, and TEM data of patient sperm.

claim: Insufficiency of CEP78 or its interacting protein causes abnormal centriole elongation and cilia shortening.
source: Insufficiency of CEP78 or its interacting protein causes abnormal centriole elongation and cilia shortening.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data from knockdown experiments.

claim: Absence of CEP78 protein in human caused similar phenotypes in vision and MMAF as Cep78−/− mice.
source: Absence of CEP78 protein in human caused similar phenotypes in vision and MMAF as Cep78−/− mice.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by comparative data from human patient and mouse model.

claim: CEP78 regulated the interaction, stability, and centriolar localization of its interacting protein.
source: Furthermore, CEP78 regulated the interaction, stability, and centriolar localization of its interacting protein.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by co-IP, western blot, and immunofluorescence data.

claim: IFT20 and TTC21A are identified as interacting proteins of CEP78.
source: Intraflagellar transport (IFT) proteins IFT20 and TTC21A are identified as interacting proteins of CEP78.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by IP-MS and co-IP data.

claim: CEP78 defects play important roles in centriole and ciliary dysfunctions and molecular pathogenesis of CRD and male infertility syndrome.
source: Collectively, our study supports the important roles of CEP78 defects in centriole and ciliary dysfunctions and molecular pathogenesis of such multi-system syndrome.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the abstract based on all experimental findings.

claim: A small portion of CRDs is due to retina cilia defects, and they may have cilia-related syndromic defects in other systems.
source: A small portion of CRDs is due to retina cilia defects, and they may have cilia-related syndromic defects in other systems (Gill et al., 2019).

claim: Pathogenic genes of CRDs with syndromic defects are associated with connecting cilia in photoreceptor, a type of non-motile cilia.
source: In this circumstance, pathogenic genes of those CRDs are associated with connecting cilia in photoreceptor, a type of non-motile cilia (Khanna et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Khanna et al., 2005.

claim: Motile and immotile cilia defects usually do not occur at the same time.
source: Motile and immotile cilia defects usually do not occur at the same time.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ciliopathies.

claim: Comprehensive analysis of the specific genetic etiology and molecular mechanism of CRD with sperm flagella abnormalities syndrome is still limited.

evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: CEP78 is exclusively expressed in ciliated organisms.

claim: The biological function of Cep78, especially its function and mechanism in CRD with male infertility, has not been well understood yet.
source: Despite these findings, the biological function of Cep78, especially its function and mechanism in CRD with male infertility, has not been well understood yet.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: To construct and maintain cilia, IFTs are recruited to the basal body and traffic proteins between cilia and the cell body.

claim: The data provide in vivo evidence for CEP78's role in maintaining structures and functions of microtubule doublets in the connecting cilium of photoreceptors.
source: Our data provide in vivo evidence for CEP78's role in maintaining structures and functions of microtubule doublets in the connecting cilium of photoreceptors.

evidence: This is a summary statement based on observations of defects in both manchette and axoneme.

claim: Interference of Cep78 led to elongation of centriole in previous in vitro studies.

source: and plays important roles in spermatogenesis and particularly spermiogenesis by transferring cargo proteins for sperm flagella formation (Zhang et al., 2016b).

source: IFT20 is essential to male fertility, spermatogenesis, and particularly spermiogenesis by transferring cargo proteins for sperm flagella formation.

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2019.

claim: Disease phenotypes and changes of ultra-structures were highly consistent between human and mice upon CEP78 depletion.
source: Disease phenotypes and changes of ultra-structures were highly consistent between human and mice upon CEP78 depletion.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on comparative data from human patient and mouse model.

source: In conclusion, we identify CEP78 as a causative gene for a type of syndrome involving CRD and male infertility.

source: The interaction between CEP78, IFT20, and TTC21A is important for the regulation of centriole and cilia length.
